title: The Antidote To A Disruptive, Immature Class
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that a class that is not badly behaved but is chronically excitable, talkative, and slow to settle is usually suffering not from a lack of consistency but from sloppily taught routines. He contends that every recurring classroom action should be converted into a highly specific routine that students perform without teacher prompting, modeled explicitly and drilled until flawless. The piece urges teachers to go far beyond a casual walkthrough, comparing the necessary attention to detail to a NASA engineer preparing a rocket launch. Routines need not be rigid or militaristic, he notes, but they must be exact and consistently enforced, with no deviation accepted once taught. The article closes by tying disciplined routines to broader academic transfer, arguing that the same standard of precision spills over into how students approach math, writing, and other subjects.
points: Chronic classroom disruption in an otherwise well-behaved class often traces back to under-taught, loosely defined routines rather than a lack of consistency.
Every repeated classroom action should be converted into a highly specific routine that students can perform without teacher direction.
Routines must be modeled explicitly, practiced until flawless, and then enforced without exception every single day.
Precision in routines does not require a militaristic tone; routines can be relaxed in style as long as the standard remains exact.
The discipline instilled through detailed routines transfers directly into students' academic work habits across every subject.
quotes: However, all-class misbehavior can often be traced back to sloppy routines. The standards of which are almost always too low and ill defined.

Everything you do repeatedly as a class, like entering the classroom, transitioning from one activity to the next, or opening laptops, should be made into a highly specific routine students do without your input.

Show your students precisely how to sit quietly and work, ask a question, line up for lunch, hang up their backpack, gather into groups, give their attention, etc. Model what it looks like. Have your class practice until they can prove to you they can do it perfectly.
And whenever they don’t mirror back the high standard you’ve set, then have them repeat the routine. Accept nothing less than excellence, and that’s what you’ll get.

The truth is that you should go overboard in teaching routines. You should be a NASA engineer preparing the Saturn V for a trip to the moon. Details can spell the difference between Apollo 1 and Apollo 11.
Having a well-behaved class is about your leadership. It’s about boldly teaching and raising expectations, even amid the reversing tides of the culture and low standards infecting our schools.
